content: The evidence for the outcome was judged to have very serious inconsistency due to the variability in reported effects across studies. One study indicated a clear effect favoring the control group, while another study reported no effect. As a result, the certainty of evidence was downgraded for inconsistency. Two studies of moderate quality were included in the analysis, but their methodological limitations, such as issues with sample comparability and outcome assessment, were noted. The effect varied between the two studies: one showed a clear effect favoring the control group, while the other showed no effect. One of the two studies used an indirect measure of the impact of marketing policy, specifically cereal price, to assess outcomes. The analysis was based on only two studies, but one study included data on 17 brands across six provinces, while the other included data on 66 cereal brands. This provided a substantial number of data points overall. Consequently, the imprecision of the evidence was deemed serious rather than very serious. The GRADE evidence profile for policies aimed at protecting children from the harmful impact of food marketing, as outlined in the WHO guideline, was referenced. The studies evaluated the impact of various marketing regulations on children’s exposure to unhealthy food advertising and their associated behaviors. Sharon Friel declared receiving a research grant from the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia (NHMRC) to fund the Centre of Research Excellence on Social Determinants of Health Equity (CRE) from 2015 to 2020. The CRE aimed to provide evidence on navigating political and policy processes to operationalize social determinants of health and health inequity. She also received a grant from NHMRC for the Australian Prevention Partnership Centre Food Project on systems approaches to healthy and equitable eating. These declarations were not deemed to constitute a conflict of interest for her role in the NUGAG Subgroup on Policy Actions, given the topics covered by the funding. Cho-il Kim declared no interests. Knut-Inge Klepp stated that his institution, the National Institute of Public Health in Norway, paid for his participation in the first meeting of the NUGAG Subgroup on Policy Actions. This was not considered a conflict of interest due to the source of the funding. Joerg Meerpohl, Musonda Mofu, and Celeste Naude declared no interests. Ladda Mo-suwan disclosed presenting at the Pre-Congress of the 20th Annual Meeting of the Pediatric Association in January 2019 on the nutritional status and dietary intake of young children in Thailand. She also participated in annual meetings of Wyeth and Abbott on infant and young child nutrition in 2016, 2017, and 2018, with expenses covered by her university. These participations were not deemed to pose a risk to the guideline development process, given the focus of the meetings. Lisa Powell declared receiving funds from WHO to travel and speak at a WHO/Pan American Health Organization meeting in 2016, participate in a meeting on fiscal policies in Barbados, attend an expert consultation in 2017, and support analysis for the Maldives. Additionally, her employer, the University of Illinois, Chicago, received an academic research grant from Bloomberg Philanthropies. These declarations were not considered conflicts of interest for her role in the NUGAG Subgroup on Policy Actions. Barbara Schneeman declared that she was employed by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) until 2012, where she contributed to the development of nutrition recommendations and represented the U.S. in Codex committees on food labeling and nutrition. She also worked with USAID as a higher education coordinator and participated in advisory roles for Monsanto, McCormick Science Institute, Ocean Spray, General Mills, DSM, Hampton Creek, and a Washington D.C. law firm on various regulatory and labeling issues. Each engagement was assessed in the context of the guideline topic and deemed unrelated to the development process.
